about: Spanish pharmaceutical company based in Barcelona, specialising in medical dermatology, with products such as Ilumetri (tildrakizumab) for psoriasis and the licensed lebrikizumab (Ebglyss) for atopic dermatitis in Europe, sold to dermatologists across Europe and the US. It is listed on the Spanish stock exchange and was founded in 1943, with revenue over 900 million euros. Prescription-focused, so mainly B2B though the name is known to Spanish consumers.

Cleveland regenerative medicine company (Nasdaq: ATHX) that developed MultiStem, an adult stem cell therapy, for ischaemic stroke and acute respiratory distress, with Healios of Japan as its partner. Late-stage stroke results fell short and the company filed for Chapter 11 in January 2024. B2B and defunct, no consumer awareness. MultiStem cells are taken from adult bone marrow and were meant to reduce inflammation after injury. Athersys was founded in 1995 and had cut staff before bankruptcy.

Boston clinical-stage oncology company (Nasdaq: IKNA) that used a platform called Kynnecta to find drug targets in tumours, with candidates such as IK-175, an AHR inhibitor, and IK-930, a TEAD inhibitor. It was funded by venture investors and an IPO in 2021, and merged with Inmagene Biopharmaceuticals in 2023 and then pivoted to a different pipeline. B2B biotech, no consumer presence.

about: American generic pharmaceutical developer and maker, with a base in the New York area, supplying oral solid doses and other generic products to wholesalers and pharmacies, mostly in the US. Customers buy under the company name and private labels. A small, low-profile generics maker with no consumer brand and limited public data. Generic drugs typically compete on price and approvals, and such firms sell to the big US drug wholesalers and retail chains. No public figures are available for revenue or headcount, which suggests a small operation.

about: Texas clinical-stage biotech developing RBT-1 for the prevention of complications after cardiac surgery such as acute kidney injury, and a programme for kidney disease. It is privately held and venture funded. Customers will eventually be cardiac surgeons and hospitals, and revenue is zero so far. B2B and pre-commercial, with no consumer profile. The kidney injury market after surgery has no approved drug today, which is the commercial opportunity it chases.

about: Watertown, Massachusetts gene editing company that developed programmable genomic integration to insert large DNA sequences at chosen locations, aiming at cell therapies and genetic diseases. It launched in 2021 with large venture funding, and shut down in 2024 after failing to raise further money. Pre-clinical and B2B, with no consumer profile. Tome was started by veterans of the CRISPR field, and its technology aimed to avoid the cutting of DNA that standard gene editing uses.

about: La Jolla algae biotechnology company, formerly Synthetic Genomics, that engineered microalgae to produce biofuels and other products, with a long partnership with ExxonMobil. It also sold bioscience products and research in the past and has used genomics to optimise productivity. Privately held, research-focused and B2B, with no consumer profile. Algae can grow on non-arable land using sunlight and carbon dioxide, which is why oil companies funded the research. Today the firm focuses on algae strains and tools for sustainable products, with limited revenue.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts biotech that studies transposable elements, the repetitive 'jumping' genes in the human genome, and their role in disease, developing drugs for autoimmune and inflammatory conditions and cancer. It is privately held with venture funding and no marketed products. B2B only, with no consumer profile. Transposable elements make up roughly half of human DNA, and the company argues they drive inflammation and cancer. It is a young firm with a small team and no products on sale.

about: Cambridge, Massachusetts biotech founded by Flagship Pioneering that develops protein nanoparticles to deliver gene editing and genetic medicines safely to targeted cells in the body. Privately held, venture-funded and pre-clinical, with partnership opportunities for pharma. B2B only and no consumer profile. Aera is a young company from Flagship, which also launched Moderna, and the approach is designed to avoid the delivery limits of viral vectors and lipid particles. It is early in development and has no products for sale.

about: Boston clinical-stage oncology company (Nasdaq: ELEV) that developed targeted cancer drugs, first seribantumab for tumours with NRG1 gene fusions, then EO-3021, an antibody-drug conjugate for gastric cancer targeting Claudin 18.2. It was loss-making with no revenue, and the programmes were later wound down or sold. B2B biotech with no consumer presence. Elevation Oncology was based in New York before moving to Boston, listed on Nasdaq in 2021 and relied entirely on equity funding rather than sales.

about: Austin health research company that runs a network of community physician practices as clinical trial sites and combines it with real-world data and technology, connecting pharmaceutical sponsors with patients in everyday care. Revenue comes from sponsor contracts and data services. Private and venture backed. B2B only, with no consumer brand. Its model puts research into familiar local doctors' offices, which is meant to enrol more diverse and rural patients than big academic centres can.

about: Phoenix nutrition and biotechnology company that makes bovine colostrum-based and immune-support ingredients, selling products such as DiaResQ for digestive health and supplying them to nutrition brands and healthcare providers. Revenue comes from ingredient sales and branded medical foods. Small privately held company. Sold mostly B2B, though DiaResQ reaches consumers. PanTheryx was founded in the 2010s and uses fermentation and processing from dairy sources to make products for digestive disorders. It works with health professionals and nutrition companies in the US and abroad.

about: Chengdu-based Chinese developer of nanopore gene sequencing technology and instruments, working to provide a domestic alternative to long-read sequencers from Oxford Nanopore for research labs, hospitals and genetic testing companies. Privately held and venture backed, with products in an early commercial stage. B2B life science tools, with little public recognition. The company is one of the new domestic sequencing instrument makers set up as China builds its own genomic technology supply chain, with a focus on real-time, portable devices and direct detection of DNA and RNA. Funding has come from technology investors.

about: Aliso Viejo medical device company that markets the mild procedure, a minimally invasive treatment for lumbar spinal stenosis that removes thickened ligament tissue, plus related devices, to spine and pain specialists in the US. Revenue comes from device sales and procedures reimbursed by Medicare. Private and venture backed. B2B healthcare with no consumer brand. Its mild procedure is performed through a small incision under imaging guidance, avoiding open surgery, which makes it attractive for elderly patients with back pain.

about: San Carlos, California clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company (Nasdaq: APGN, via a 2022 SPAC) developing sotigalimab, a CD40 antibody for immunotherapy of pancreatic cancer and other tumours. It had no revenue, struggled to fund trials and entered bankruptcy proceedings around 2023-2024. B2B biotech with no consumer profile. Sotigalimab is an antibody designed to activate immune cells and had been tested in combination with chemotherapy. Apexigen had earlier worked with Roche and others.

about: Philadelphia biotech developing tissue-targeted genetic medicines using Centyrin protein scaffolds, a technology linked to Janssen, to deliver siRNA and other payloads to specific cell types. Privately held and venture funded. Pre-clinical, with partnerships being its route to revenue. B2B only, with no consumer exposure. Centyrins were originally developed as an alternative to antibodies, and Aro is working on gene-silencing and gene-delivery medicines aimed at tissues such as muscle, liver or lungs.

about: Pennsylvania clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: GRTX) developing avasopasem manganese, a superoxide dismutase mimetic to reduce severe oral mucositis in head and neck cancer patients receiving radiation. The FDA declined approval in 2023 and the company cut costs heavily. B2B biotech, with no consumer profile and no marketed products. Galera was founded in 2012 and listed on Nasdaq in 2019. Radiation mucositis causes painful mouth sores that interrupt cancer treatment, so the market is real, but approval remains a hurdle.

about: Quebec health and wellness company (Nasdaq: NEPT) that began as a krill oil omega-3 supplier, then moved into consumer packaged goods, buying Sprout Foods, a baby food brand, in 2021, and selling cannabis and wellness products. It was loss-making, shrank through divestments, and went through insolvency proceedings in 2024. Consumer brand Sprout is sold at US retailers. Neptune is based in Laval. Its stock was moved from the TSX to Nasdaq only, and it attracted attention for its repeated reverse stock splits.

Boston and Freising, Germany biotechnology company (Nasdaq: PIRS) developing Anticalin proteins, a class of small engineered molecules for cancer and respiratory disease, in collaboration with partners such as Boehringer Ingelheim and Seagen. It receives milestone and collaboration revenue, with no marketed drugs. It merged with Palvella Therapeutics in 2024. B2B with no consumer profile. Pieris was founded in Germany in 2001 and is based in Boston for US operations.

about: Amsterdam gene therapy company developing vectorised antibodies, using AAV vectors to deliver antibody genes to the brain and central nervous system for diseases such as ALS and Alzheimer's disease. Privately held and venture funded, with pre-clinical programmes. B2B only and no consumer profile. The company is a spin-out of Dutch gene therapy research, VectorY was founded in 2020 and has raised funds from investors including Forbion. It has not yet reached the clinic or had product sales.

about: Boston-area biotech developing gildeuretinol, a deuterated vitamin A analogue, to slow vision loss in Stargardt disease and dry age-related macular degeneration. Privately held and venture funded, with late-stage trials. Customers would be ophthalmologists. B2B and pre-commercial, with no consumer visibility. Stargardt disease is a rare inherited eye disease that usually starts in children and teenagers and currently has no approved therapy. Alkeus is run as a start-up focused on one lead asset rather than a broad pipeline.

about: New Jersey medical company (Nasdaq: BLPH) developing INOpulse, a portable inhaled nitric oxide system for patients with pulmonary hypertension linked to lung disease. Trial setbacks and lack of funding led to wind-down around 2023-2024. B2B medical device developer with no consumer awareness. Bellerophon was spun out of Ikaria, the maker of INOmax, and its technology draws on that history. The company's trials in pulmonary hypertension failed to hit goals and it ran out of money.

about: San Diego life sciences company that developed the Maverick, a silicon photonic diagnostic system able to run many immunoassay tests from a tiny blood sample at once, for use by labs and drug developers. Privately held and venture funded. B2B diagnostics with no consumer profile. Genalyte's systems were aimed at both infectious disease and autoimmune tests, and it was backed by venture investors.

about: Israeli clinical-stage company (NYSE American: PHGE) developing bacteriophage therapies, viruses that kill specific bacteria, to treat chronic infections in cystic fibrosis and diabetic foot osteomyelitis, with products such as BX004 and BX211. Pre-revenue and funded by equity raises. B2B, with no consumer visibility. BiomX uses a platform of natural and engineered phages to target specific bacteria linked to chronic infection and disease, and entered the US market through a SPAC listing in 2019. It runs trials in Israel and the US.

Cambridge-based synthetic DNA manufacturer, listed on AIM and the Frankfurt exchange, using enzymatic processes to produce high-fidelity DNA at large scale for use in mRNA and gene therapy production. Customers are biotech and pharma developers. It is a small company with R&D in the UK and operations in Germany. B2B only. The synthetic route avoids bacteria and can speed up the production of DNA templates needed for mRNA and gene therapy, with 4basebio also developing its own delivery systems for gene therapies.

San Diego clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: AARD) developing ARD-101, an oral gut-restricted bitter taste receptor agonist for hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome, with a metabolic disease platform. It listed in 2025 and has no marketed products. B2B only, with no consumer profile. Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disease that causes constant hunger, with few options for patients and families. Few treatments exist for it.

South Korean biotech listed on KOSDAQ, building bispecific antibodies using its Grabody platform, including programmes for cancer and brain disease. It has major licensing deals with Sanofi and GSK, and works with Compass Therapeutics and others. Revenue is mostly milestone and licence payments. B2B only, with limited consumer visibility. Grabody-B is designed to carry drugs across the blood-brain barrier, a hard problem for antibody medicines.

Baoji Pharmaceutical is a Chinese biopharma and biotechnology company with Shanghai listed as its location, according to the input. No product detail or ownership data is available. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

California dental laser company that developed the Waterlase laser systems and diode lasers for dentists, sold in North America, Europe and Asia, with consumables and service revenue. Listed on Nasdaq (BIOL), it was loss-making for years and entered bankruptcy in 2024, with assets sold. Sold to dentists, so B2B, though patients know the laser dentistry concept. Its lasers are used for hard and soft tissue procedures and aim to reduce pain, drilling and anaesthesia. Biolase was founded in 1987 and grew through dental distributors such as Henry Schein.

Australian neuroscience biotech listed on the ASX and later Nasdaq (BNOX), developing BNC210, a drug for social anxiety disorder and PTSD. It has no marketed products and relies on clinical trial funding. It merged with Neuphoria in 2025. B2B with no consumer profile. Bionomics was founded in Adelaide in 1996 and has reorganised its trials through a US Nasdaq listing.

Belgian clinical-stage biotech developing arsenic trioxide-based therapies for autoimmune and inflammatory conditions such as graft versus host disease and systemic sclerosis. Listed on Euronext Brussels and Paris. Pre-revenue and B2B, with no consumer profile. BioSenic's lead product ATO is being tested for chronic graft-versus-host disease, a serious complication of stem cell transplants, and the company is a small Walloon biotech whose shares trade in Brussels and Paris.

Philadelphia clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: CNTX) developing hormone-targeted therapies for women's cancers such as breast cancer, including a progesterone receptor antagonist (onapristone) and a bispecific antibody for solid tumours. Pre-revenue, funded by equity. B2B only, no consumer profile. The company was founded in 2015 and went public in 2021. Its strategy of targeting progesterone receptors in breast and other cancers differs from the common use of oestrogen blockers.

Georgia medical device company (Nasdaq: FEMY) selling FemaSeed, a device for intratubal insemination for infertility, FemVue for checking fallopian tube patency, and developing FemBloc, a non-surgical permanent birth control. Customers are fertility clinics and gynaecologists. Revenue is small. B2B, with limited consumer awareness. Femasys was founded in 2004 and listed on Nasdaq in 2021. The potential product, FemBloc, is designed to be an in-office alternative to surgical tubal ligation, which is a large market.

Israeli clinical-stage pharma (Nasdaq: GLMD) developing aramchol, an oral drug for fatty liver disease and fibrosis (NASH/MASH). A Phase 3 programme did not meet its main goal, after which it looked for alternatives. No product revenue. B2B and no consumer visibility. Galmed is based in Tel Aviv, listed on Nasdaq in 2014 and has a small team. Fatty liver disease affects a very large number of people, and no drug of its kind is widely approved.

Georgia biotech (Nasdaq: GOVX) developing vaccines and immunotherapies using its MVA-VLP platform for COVID-19, mpox and cancer, with a government-funded programme. Revenue is small, from grants and contracts. B2B only and little public awareness. GeoVax's MVA-based vaccine has been supported by US government funding. The company has been in a long period of development, with clinical trials of the cancer therapy and vaccines yet to deliver approvals.

French orthopaedic implant company that developed the Jazz system, a spinal fixation system using flexible bands, and instruments, sold to surgeons and hospitals. Listed on Euronext Growth in Paris and later had financial trouble and restructured. B2B medical devices, with no consumer awareness. Implanet, based near Bordeaux, derived most revenue from the sale of Jazz products and also had a US subsidiary, but it was small and shared a market with large implant companies.

Shanghai biopharmaceutical company developing and producing peptide drugs, including GLP-1 diabetes and obesity medicines, selling to hospitals in China and licensing candidates. Listed. B2B pharma, and low brand awareness outside the industry. Innogen aims at the large Chinese diabetes market, where GLP-1 drugs are in rapid growth. It sells to Chinese hospitals and is relatively new compared to large peers.

Gaithersburg clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: NEXI) developing T cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disease using its AIM nanoparticle platform. It struggled to fund trials and wound down around 2023-2024. B2B and no consumer profile. NexImmune was started with technology from Johns Hopkins and tried to make artificial antigen-presenting cells to direct T cells towards tumours and autoimmune targets. Its stock fell sharply.

Israeli clinical-stage oncology company (Nasdaq: PPBT) developing CM-24, an anti-CEACAM1 antibody, and NT219, a drug aimed at overcoming cancer drug resistance. Pre-revenue with no marketed products. B2B only, and little public awareness. Purple Biotech was formerly named Kitov Pharma and is based in Tel Aviv, with research in Israel, and it receives its funding mostly through Nasdaq share sales and has limited cash.

San Diego clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: SKYE) developing nimacimab, a CB1 antibody for obesity, from a cannabinoid-based research history. Pre-revenue and funded by equity. B2B only, no consumer profile. Skye was formerly named Emerald Bioscience and has shifted focus several times, from cannabinoid ideas to metabolic disease. The nimacimab approach is meant to block the CB1 receptor in peripheral tissues and so help with weight loss in conjunction with GLP-1 drugs.

Swedish biotech listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, developing C21 (buloxibutid), an angiotensin II type 2 receptor agonist for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other lung disease. Pre-revenue, with licensing options. B2B only and no consumer visibility. Vicore is a Swedish company, with C21 in a Phase 2 trial in IPF, and it also worked on a programme for COVID-19 lung disease earlier.

Virginia biotech (Nasdaq: ADTX) that sells AditxtScore immune monitoring tests to labs and health systems and develops Aditxt immune reprogramming therapies for autoimmune conditions and transplant rejection. It acquired and incubated several small ventures, and its revenue is very small compared with its losses. It sells to hospitals, labs and research partners, and has no consumer-facing business, making it a low-profile micro-cap that raises capital frequently through share sales.

Houston clinical-stage oncology company (Nasdaq: BPTH) that developed liposomal antisense drugs, notably prexigebersen (BP1001) for acute myeloid leukaemia and other blood cancers, built on technology licensed from MD Anderson Cancer Center. It has no marketed products and is funded by equity placements, with a small team. B2B drug developer, no consumer profile, and its trials have progressed slowly because of limited capital.

Israeli medical device company, with a US base in Burlington, Massachusetts, that makes the Deep TMS system, a non-invasive magnetic stimulation helmet cleared by the FDA for major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder and smoking cessation. It sells or leases systems to psychiatric clinics and hospitals and earns recurring treatment fees. Listed on Nasdaq (BWAY) and the Tel Aviv exchange, with revenue of roughly 40 to 50 million dollars. Known mostly to psychiatrists, with growing patient awareness.

about: Swedish clinical-stage biotech, listed on Nasdaq First North in Stockholm and based in Gothenburg, developing CS1 (valproic acid) for pulmonary arterial hypertension and thrombosis-related diseases, aiming to treat disease through epigenetic effects rather than blood-thinning. Pre-revenue and funded by share issues, with trials in Europe and the US. B2B pharma developer with no consumer profile. The company was founded in 2012 and has long-term research links to Swedish universities.

Maryland regenerative medicine and device company (Nasdaq: ELUT), formerly Aziyo Biologics, that makes biologic envelopes, such as CanGaroo, to hold cardiac implantable devices like pacemakers and reduce infection risk, plus the EluPro antibacterial envelope and orthopaedic and soft tissue products. Customers are hospitals and device manufacturers, and revenue is in the tens of millions of dollars. B2B med-tech, with no consumer recognition.

Danish biotech from Hørsholm, listed on Nasdaq First North in Copenhagen, that uses its ExpreS2 insect-cell protein expression platform to make complex vaccine antigens, with malaria and COVID-19 vaccine projects and a partnership model with research groups and vaccine developers. Revenue comes from contract services and grants. B2B life science company with no consumer profile. ExpreS2ion was founded in 2010 and is run from Denmark's Medicon Valley.

South Korean biotech listed on KOSDAQ, working on antiviral and anti-cancer candidates built around niclosamide-based drugs and other repurposed compounds, with trials in Korea and abroad. Revenue is small. It is unrelated to Hyundai Motor Group despite the name. B2B drug developer, with low public awareness. It operates from Seoul and sits among a large group of Korean small-cap biotechs, with trials in oncology and respiratory diseases and a modest scale of operations.

South Korean immuno-oncology biotech based in Gyeonggi province developing antibody-based and cell therapies for cancer and immune diseases, listed on the KOSDAQ market. Revenue comes mainly from licensing and research contracts, and it has no marketed product. B2B biotech with minimal consumer awareness. Its development programmes sit in the antibody and cell therapy area, and it conducts research in Suwon, a city with a strong biotech and electronics cluster. Customers would be pharmaceutical partners buying licences, and hospitals if products are approved.

Sydney-based immunotherapy company, listed on the ASX and Nasdaq (IMMP), developing eftilagimod alpha, a soluble LAG-3 protein that activates antigen-presenting cells, in combination with Merck's Keytruda for lung and head and neck cancer, with partners including Merck, Merck KGaA and Pfizer, and licence revenue from GSK. Pre-commercial with no product sales. B2B with no consumer profile. Immutep is led from Sydney and runs trials in Europe and the US.

La Jolla biopharma (Nasdaq: LBPH) developing bexicaserin, a 5-HT2C agonist for developmental and epileptic encephalopathies such as Dravet syndrome. Danish drugmaker Lundbeck acquired Longboard in late 2024 for about 2.6 billion dollars. Clinical-stage with no revenue and no consumer profile, aimed at neurologists treating rare childhood epilepsies. Dravet syndrome is a rare, severe childhood epilepsy, and the company's candidate is designed to avoid heart valve risks seen in older drugs. Lundbeck's purchase brought a late-stage neurology asset into its portfolio.

Virginia fibre-optic sensing company (Nasdaq: LUNA) selling ODiSI sensors that use optical fibre to measure strain and temperature in aerospace, automotive and energy testing, as well as photonics test products and, earlier, government contract research. It had revenue of roughly 100 million dollars before a restatement and delisting problems. B2B technology supplier, with no consumer profile. Luna was founded in 1990 and later sold or reorganised parts of the business.

Finnish nanotechnology and pharmaceutical engineering company, listed on Nasdaq First North in Helsinki, that uses its CESS supercritical fluid technology to shrink poorly soluble drug molecules into nanoparticles that dissolve better. Customers are pharma firms paying for development projects and sometimes taking licences, and it also advances its own pipeline. B2B drug delivery specialist, with no consumer profile. Nanoform was founded in 2015 and spun out of research at the University of Helsinki.

Maryland cell and gene therapy company (Nasdaq: ORGS) built around its point-of-care model, in which therapies are made near the patient, with a development and manufacturing network of hospital partners in the US, Europe and Asia and a regenerative medicine licensing business. Revenue is small and has come from contract manufacturing and licensing. B2B only, with limited public awareness. Orgenesis is headquartered in Germantown, Maryland, and operates internationally.

South Korean biopharma developing diagnostics and treatments for neurodegenerative disease and other conditions, listed on KOSDAQ and based in Seongnam. It sells to hospitals and labs and partners with research institutes. B2B life science company, with limited public awareness. PeopleBio is a small Korean developer in the Seongnam area, close to Pangyo, the country's technology and biotech cluster. It is an early-stage company, and any product revenue would come mainly from diagnostics and hospital customers.

Texas wound care and surgical products company (Nasdaq: SMTI) selling CellerateRX, BIAKOS antimicrobial wound products and other advanced wound care items, to physicians, hospitals and surgical centres. Revenue is about 70 to 100 million dollars. B2B healthcare supplier with no consumer brand. Sanara MedTech has grown through acquisitions and licensing, and relies on a specialist sales force that visits wound clinics, nursing facilities and surgeons. Its products are mainly reimbursed through hospital and clinic purchases.

North Carolina biotech contract manufacturer (Nasdaq: SCPX), formerly NightHawk Biosciences, which bought the former Heat Biologics business and operates a CDMO for biologics and viral vectors from a plant in San Antonio, Texas. It sells manufacturing services to biotech and pharma customers. B2B with no consumer profile. Scorpius also provides analytical and fill-finish capabilities and serves clients that need clinical-stage manufacturing of biologic drugs.

Austin biotech (Nasdaq: TFFP) developing inhaled dry powder drugs using its Thin Film Freezing technology, including vaccines and antivirals, with partnerships with universities and drug makers. Revenue is minimal. B2B drug delivery developer, with no consumer visibility. Its Thin Film Freezing creates powders that can be inhaled, for example against lung infections. TFF also tests its approach with partners such as the University of Texas. The company has had no product launches.

California late-stage pharma (Nasdaq: UNCY) developing oxylanthanum carbonate, a phosphate binder for hyperphosphatemia in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis, aimed at a market dominated by Sanofi's Renvela and others. Pre-revenue. B2B, selling to nephrologists and dialysis operators in future. No consumer profile. Unicycive was founded in 2016 and reports to investors from California. The company has faced FDA manufacturing issues for its lead product.

Rochester, New York clinical-stage biotech (Nasdaq: VCNX) developing pepinemab, an antibody against semaphorin 4D, in Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease and cancer, with a partnership with Merck KGaA. Pre-revenue. B2B and no consumer profile. Vaccinex was founded in 2001 and went public in 2018. Its antibody pepinemab was tested in Huntington's disease and showed some signals, but regulatory progress needs more data.

French biotech listed on Euronext Paris developing glenzocimab, an antibody that blocks platelet glycoprotein VI to treat acute ischaemic stroke without increasing bleeding risk. Pre-revenue, with trials in Europe. B2B and no consumer profile. Acticor was founded in 2013 as a spin-out from French research institutes and its drug is designed to be given in ambulances or at hospital admission. Stroke is a major cause of death and disability, so a safe clot treatment would be significant.

Atlanta biotech (NYSE American: ALZN) developing lithium-based AL001 for Alzheimer's disease and a vaccine for the same disease, licensed from the University of South Florida. Pre-revenue. B2B and no consumer profile. Alzamend is based in Atlanta, with a small team, and it lists on the NYSE American. Its lithium formulation aims to reduce the side effects of older lithium treatments. It also works on a vaccine for Alzheimer's.

Applied UV was a manufacturer of ultraviolet disinfection systems under the SteriLumen brand and of hospitality furniture through MunnWorks, selling to hospitals, schools and hotels. Listed on Nasdaq (AUVI), it struggled financially and filed for bankruptcy in 2024. Defunct B2B company with no consumer brand. Its UV disinfection range was marketed for hospitals, schools and hotels during COVID-19 and shrank afterwards.

Danish biotech from Kongens Lyngby that makes Aquaporin Inside membranes, which use biomimetic water channel proteins to filter water for desalination, industrial reuse and space applications. Customers are industrial and water treatment firms. Listed on Nasdaq First North, with a small revenue. B2B and not a consumer brand. The company was founded in 2005 and is based in Kongens Lyngby near Copenhagen, working with water research teams in Denmark and Singapore.

Puerto Rico-based biopharma that listed on Nasdaq (ASBP) in 2025 and is developing sublingual and intravenous aspirin formulations aimed at faster onset for heart attack and pain. Pre-revenue, with limited public history. B2B and little consumer awareness. Aspire's stated plan is to use a fast-acting aspirin product for emergencies such as a suspected heart attack. It is a small company with limited disclosure.

Chinese vaccine maker in Chengdu best known for human diploid cell rabies vaccines, a premium product sold to provincial disease control centres and clinics in China, and also developing other vaccines and veterinary products. Listed on a mainland China exchange. B2B and government sales, with limited consumer recognition. The firm is based in Chengdu, in Sichuan province, and has built its brand on quality rabies vaccines.

Georgia pain-focused biotech (Nasdaq: DWTX), formerly Virios Therapeutics, developing Halneuron, a non-opioid nerve blocker for chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain, and a long COVID programme. Pre-revenue and funded by equity. B2B and no consumer profile. Dogwood changed its name in 2024 and relies on small clinical trials funded by investors. Neuropathic pain after chemotherapy affects many cancer patients and has few good treatments.

Danish medical technology company, listed on Nasdaq First North in Stockholm, developing fluorescent imaging agents to help surgeons see tumours during operations, with its lead product being tested in cancers such as prostate and brain. Pre-revenue. B2B and no consumer profile. FluoGuide's lead product, FG001, targets uPAR, a protein found in many aggressive cancers. The surgical-imaging approach is aimed at helping surgeons remove all cancer tissue.

Australian molecular diagnostics company, listed on the ASX and Nasdaq (GENE), selling GeneType genetic risk tests for breast cancer and other diseases, with its customers being clinicians and labs. Revenue is small. B2B and little consumer awareness. Genetic Technologies is based in Melbourne, and its tests are sold to doctors and through health professionals in the US, Australia and Europe.

Swiss biotech from Geneva, listed on Euronext Paris, developing antibodies such as temelimab against a human endogenous retrovirus envelope protein, for multiple sclerosis and other conditions, with partnerships earlier with Servier. Pre-revenue, B2B only. GeNeuro's antibodies target the HERV-W envelope protein, which scientists link to the inflammation seen in MS. Pre-revenue. The company has a small team and relies on external funding for trials.

Japanese consumer health and household products maker, listed in Tokyo (4967), best known for Netsusama Sheet fever cooling gel patches, Bluelet toilet cleaner, Sawaday air fresheners and Ice Non, plus supplements and personal care. It sells through drugstores and supermarkets across Japan, with growing exports to Asia. Revenue is above 150 billion yen. Founded in 1919. Strong household brands in Japan.

Swedish medical technology company from Uppsala, listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, selling OssDsign Cranial, a bone graft implant for repairing skull defects, and Catalyst, a bone graft for spinal fusion and other procedures. Customers are neurosurgeons and hospitals in Europe and the US. B2B med-tech with no consumer profile. OssDsign was founded in 2012 and spun out of Uppsala University research on calcium phosphate bone grafts. It sells through direct sales and distributors.

Pharos iBio is a South Korean biotechnology and health care company based in Anyang, Gyeonggi-do, which is listed according to the input. The record gives no pipeline, products or ownership details. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

Norwegian medical isotope company, listed on Euronext Growth Oslo, producing thorium-228 and radium-224 to supply lead-212 for targeted alpha cancer therapy, making use of naturally occurring raw material. Customers are developers of radiopharmaceuticals. Pre-commercial scale. B2B only and no consumer profile. Thor Medical uses naturally decaying raw material to produce radioisotopes that are rare and in short supply, which matters for cancer therapy developers.

UK veterinary pharmaceutical company in York, listed on AIM, that develops, licenses and sells animal health products for pets and livestock, including pet anaesthetics, medicines for horses and pain products, sold through vets and wholesalers across Europe. Revenue is in the tens of millions of pounds. B2B animal health supplier, with little public brand recognition. Animalcare also distributes products for other animal health companies.

German specialty pharma company from Leverkusen, listed in Frankfurt and on Nasdaq (BFRI), best known for Ameluz, a gel used with red light in photodynamic therapy for actinic keratosis, a precancerous skin condition, and BF-RhodoLED lamps, sold to dermatologists in the US and Europe. Revenue is about 40 to 50 million dollars. B2B dermatology products. Biofrontera's brand is well recognised in its niche among dermatologists and private clinics.

California specialty pharma (Nasdaq: EVOK) selling Gimoti, a nasal spray of metoclopramide, for adults with diabetic gastroparesis, a stomach emptying disorder, in the US through specialty channels, with revenue of a few million dollars. Founded in 2007. B2B with prescriptions driven by gastroenterologists and a little direct patient marketing. The product is reimbursed by insurance and sold through specialty pharmacies. Evoke has a small commercial team and its revenue depends on a single product.

Finnish biotech from Espoo, listed on Nasdaq First North, developing HER-096, a small peptide drug for Parkinson's disease aimed at protecting neurons, from its earlier work on neurotrophic factors. Pre-revenue. B2B and no consumer profile. Herantis was founded in 2008 and is a spinout from Finnish research. Its market capitalisation is small, and it depends on investor funding to run trials.

Minnesota contract development and manufacturing organisation for sterile injectable drugs and hyaluronic acid, filling syringes and vials for pharma customers in the US. It is the former Landec (Nasdaq: LFCR) after exiting its food business, and acquired the original Lifecore business in 2010. Revenue is about 100 million dollars. B2B, with no consumer profile. Lifecore specialises in difficult filling of sterile products, serving large pharma customers.

Swedish clinical-stage biotech from Stockholm, listed on Nasdaq First North, developing sevuparin to treat sepsis-related organ damage and other severe conditions. Pre-revenue. B2B and no consumer profile. Modus was founded in 2012 as a spin-out from Uppsala University research. Sepsis is a life-threatening condition for which there are few specific treatments. It has no marketed products. Its shares trade on a small-cap market.
OPM Biosciences is a Shanghai-based biopharma and biotechnology company, listed according to the input. No products or pipeline are specified. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

Utah regenerative medicine company (Nasdaq: PTE) that developed SkinTE, an autologous skin graft product grown from a patient's own tissue, and ran wound care and related businesses. It never achieved significant sales, and filed for bankruptcy in 2023. B2B and defunct, with no consumer profile. PolarityTE was based in Salt Lake City, with an investor base from retail shareholders. Its strategy was to build new skin from small samples of patient tissue.

Australian RNA therapeutics company, listed on the ASX, developing peptide-based drugs for genetic diseases of the eye and kidney, such as autosomal dominant optic atrophy and polycystic kidney disease. Pre-revenue. B2B with no consumer profile. PYC Therapeutics is based in Perth, with US operations in San Francisco. Optic atrophy is an inherited disease that affects the optic nerve and can lead to blindness. The company is developing its drugs with the help of drug-delivery technology.

Oxford-based UK biotech, listed on AIM, developing cancer immunotherapies including Immunobody DNA vaccines and the Moditope platform, with lead candidate iSCIB1+ for melanoma. Pre-revenue. B2B only, with no consumer visibility. The company's lead program is being tested alongside standard checkpoint therapy and is run from Oxford and Glasgow, with a few dozen staff. Scancell was founded in 1997. It has run trials in the UK.

London-based diagnostics company (Nasdaq: VRAX) developing T-cell-based immune response tests and sells viral test kits for the detection of infections, listed in 2022. Revenue is small. B2B and little consumer awareness. Virax Biolabs has operations in London and Hong Kong and sells to labs, clinics and distributors. It focuses on respiratory infections such as COVID-19, and on T-cell testing. It is small.

Nimbus Therapeutics is a US biotechnology company using computational chemistry and physics-based design to create small-molecule drugs for hard-to-target proteins, working with Schrödinger. Its programmes include metabolic and immunology targets. A TYK2 inhibitor programme was sold to Takeda in 2022, a landmark licensing deal worth billions. Funded by venture investors and pharma partners. Private R&D company with no consumer profile.

about: US specialty pharmaceutical company known for oral ADHD medicines, including Adzenys XR-ODT and Cotempla XR-ODT extended-release orally disintegrating tablets, and Adzenys ER liquid suspension. Patients are mainly children and adolescents, and products are prescribed by paediatricians and psychiatrists and sold through US pharmacies. Based in Texas, it was listed on Nasdaq and merged with Aytu BioScience in 2021. Pharma brand with moderate recognition among prescribers and none among the general public.

about: US medical technology company developing shockwave therapies for wound care and tissue repair, notably the UltraMIST ultrasound system for treating chronic wounds and the dermaPACE device for diabetic foot ulcers. Customers are hospitals, wound care centres and clinics, with sales through distributors. Based in the Atlanta area, with a mixed record of profits. Medical brand with no consumer profile, though known among wound care clinicians.

Swedish generic pharmaceutical company listed on Nasdaq First North that develops, registers and sells generic medicines, including pain, heart and other prescription drugs, to Nordic and European pharmacies and hospitals. Customers are wholesalers, pharmacies and public purchasers. Revenue comes from generic drug sales and has grown through new product launches and tender wins. Small pharma firm with moderate recognition among Nordic pharmacists and none among consumers.

US specialty pharmaceutical company best known for Xifaxan, a gastrointestinal antibiotic used for travellers' diarrhoea, hepatic encephalopathy and irritable bowel syndrome, alongside Relistor, Apriso and other gastro drugs. Customers are gastroenterologists and patients through pharmacies. Founded in the 1990s, it was bought by Valeant Pharmaceuticals (now Bausch Health) in 2015 for about 10.4 billion USD and is now Bausch's Salix unit. B2B pharma brand with strong awareness among gastroenterologists.

about: South Korean biosimilar developer, a joint venture formed in 2012 by Samsung BioLogics and Biogen, now fully Samsung-owned after Biogen sold its stake in 2022. Markets biosimilars in Europe and the US, including Benepali (etanercept), Imraldi (adalimumab), Flixabi (infliximab), Ontruzant (trastuzumab) and ustekinumab versions, through partners such as Organon, Biogen and Sandoz. Customers are hospitals and payers. Operates from Songdo, Incheon, with sales in Europe and the US. B2B pharma brand with no consumer profile.

Belgian biotechnology company that pioneered Nanobodies, small antibody-derived therapeutic proteins based on camelid heavy-chain antibodies. Its lead product, caplacizumab (Cablivi), treats acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Partnered with Merck KGaA, AbbVie, Boehringer Ingelheim and Sanofi, which acquired the company in 2018 for about 3.9 billion euros. Customers are hospitals and pharma partners. Research-led B2B company with no consumer awareness, now part of Sanofi.

US biotechnology company that developed drugs for rare diseases and complement-mediated disorders, starting with hepatitis C antivirals and moving to complement factor D inhibitors such as danicopan, for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Listed on Nasdaq (ACHN). Acquired by Alexion in early 2020 for about 930 million USD, after which danicopan reached the market. Research-based pharma with no consumer awareness and a niche patient community.

US life sciences and diagnostics tools company, spun out of Hewlett-Packard in 1999 and listed on the NYSE (A). Sells liquid and gas chromatography, mass spectrometers, genomic and cell analysis instruments, software and services to pharmaceutical, chemical, food and environmental laboratories worldwide. Revenue is around 6 to 7 billion USD, with roughly 18,000 employees, and a large share comes from consumables and services. B2B brand with strong visibility in laboratories and among scientists.

US specialty pharmaceutical company that sold Makena (hydroxyprogesterone caproate) to reduce preterm birth risk, Feraheme for iron-deficiency anaemia, and Intrarosa for painful intercourse due to menopause. Customers are obstetricians, hospitals and women's health clinics. Listed on Nasdaq (AMAG), it ran into trouble when Makena's effectiveness was challenged, and was acquired by Covis Pharma in 2020 for about 647 million USD. Moderate awareness among prescribers, little among consumers.

US oncology biopharmaceutical company, listed on Nasdaq (EXEL), best known for Cabometyx and Cometriq (cabozantinib), a kinase inhibitor used for kidney, liver and thyroid cancers, and for royalties on partnered products. Revenue is above 1.5 billion USD a year, driven mainly by US cabozantinib sales and licensing. Developing further oncology compounds and expanding into other cancers. Founded in the 1990s as a drug discovery company. Strong brand among oncologists, little consumer awareness.

Danish pharmaceutical group focused on dermatology, with treatments for psoriasis, atopic dermatitis and actinic keratosis, including Enstilar, Adtralza (tralokinumab) and Picato, and a pipeline in medical dermatology. Customers are dermatologists and patients across more than 100 countries. Founded in 1908 and owned by the LEO Foundation, which funds scientific research, so it is not listed. Roughly 4,000 employees and revenue of about 1.5 billion euros. Brand well known to dermatologists, with some consumer familiarity in Europe.

US oncology biotech focused on targeted cancer drugs for genetically defined tumours, led by larotrectinib (Vitrakvi), the first tissue-agnostic therapy for TRK fusion cancers, and selpercatinib (Retevmo) for RET-driven cancers. Customers were oncologists and patients globally. Listed on Nasdaq (LOXO) and acquired by Eli Lilly in early 2019 for about 8 billion USD. A research-driven company with high standing among cancer specialists but no public awareness.

Mojave Pharma is a US pharmaceutical company based in Las Vegas, Nevada, which Crunchbase describes as focused on researching novel therapies, tagged under biotechnology and health care. The input does not support specific products, pipeline, ownership or scale. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: US biopharmaceutical company that developed boron-based small molecule drugs, including tavaborole (Kerydin) for toenail fungus and crisaborole (Eucrisa) for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis. Customers were dermatologists, with products sold in US pharmacies. Listed on Nasdaq (ANAC) and acquired by Pfizer in 2016 for about 5.2 billion USD. Strong reputation in dermatology drug discovery, no consumer brand of its own now.

US precision medicine company, listed on Nasdaq (ARRY), which developed targeted cancer drugs including binimetinib (Mektovi) and encorafenib (Braftovi) for BRAF-mutated melanoma and colorectal cancer. Also earned collaboration revenue from partners such as Novartis and Pfizer. Customers were oncologists and patients through pharmacies. Acquired by Pfizer in 2019 for about 11.4 billion USD. Founded in 1998 and headquartered in Boulder, Colorado. Strong scientific brand in oncology, little consumer awareness.

Indonesia's state-owned vaccine and biopharmaceutical producer, founded in 1890 in Bandung and now the parent of Indonesia's state-owned healthcare holding. Makes vaccines for polio, measles, hepatitis B and others, supplies the national immunisation programme, and produced COVID-19 vaccines with partners such as Sinovac. Customers are the Indonesian government, health agencies and exports to dozens of countries. Strong national brand within Indonesia, little consumer advertising.

US RNA interference therapeutics company known for its GalXC platform, producing medicines such as lumasiran (Oxlumo) for primary hyperoxaluria and nedosiran. Collaborated with Roche, Eli Lilly, Alexion and Novo Nordisk. Listed on Nasdaq (DRNA) and acquired by Novo Nordisk in late 2021 for about 3.3 billion USD. Customers are patients with rare liver diseases through pharma partners. Research-driven company with no consumer visibility.

Genuity Science is a genomics and data analytics company with offices in Boston and Dublin, tagged in Crunchbase under analytics, artificial intelligence and biotechnology. It appears to combine genetic sequencing and large health datasets for research and drug discovery customers. Ownership, products and scale cannot be confirmed from the input. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Chinese drugmaker based in Dongguan, Guangdong, part of the HEC Group, producing branded and generic medicines through its Sunshine Lake Pharma business, including antivirals, cardiovascular, respiratory and metabolic drugs, with a growing innovative pipeline. Customers are hospitals and distributors in China, plus exports of active ingredients. Privately held with a history of selling to global markets. B2B pharma brand with little consumer awareness.
cb_desc: HEC Pharm is a Chinese drugmaker company.

about: US oncology biotechnology company known for entrectinib (Rozlytrek), a targeted therapy for ROS1-positive lung cancer and NTRK fusion-positive solid tumours, plus related precision cancer drugs in its pipeline. Listed on Nasdaq (RXDX) and acquired by Roche in early 2018 for about 1.7 billion USD. Customers were oncologists and patients who are matched to the drug by genetic testing. Research-driven company with no consumer awareness, now integrated into Roche and Genentech.

US biopharmaceutical company that developed Trulance (plecanatide), a once-daily pill for chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, launched in the US in 2017. Listed on Nasdaq (SGYP). Customers were gastroenterologists and primary care physicians, with patients buying through pharmacies. Filed for bankruptcy in December 2018, after which its assets, including Trulance, were acquired by Bausch Health. Small specialty pharma brand with a short commercial life.

US vaccine developer using its MAPS technology to create multivalent pneumococcal conjugate vaccines that could protect against more strains than existing shots. Customers would be public health systems and patients through pharma partners. Backed by venture investors, it was acquired by GSK in 2022 for about 2.1 billion USD upfront plus milestones. Research-stage company with no public awareness, now integrated into GSK's vaccines unit.

US biotechnology company, listed on Nasdaq (ABUS), working on a cure for chronic hepatitis B and on coronavirus therapies, with expertise in lipid nanoparticle delivery technology licensed to Moderna and others, including for Onpattro-class RNA medicines. Revenue comes from licensing and royalties, plus collaborations. Based in the Philadelphia area. Research company with a Canadian origin, known to biotech investors and virologists but not to the public.

US biotechnology company that used single-cell sequencing to discover antibodies from patients' immune cells, aiming to develop cancer immunotherapies, notably ATRC-101 for solid tumours. Listed on Nasdaq (BCEL) in 2019, it was based in South San Francisco and wound down operations in 2023 after clinical results disappointed. Customers would have been pharma partners and, eventually, oncologists and patients. Research-stage firm with no consumer profile.

about: Canadian biotech company focused on camlipixant, a P2X3 receptor antagonist in late-stage trials for refractory chronic cough, and previously worked on rare disease and pain treatments. Listed on Nasdaq and the TSX (BLU) and based near Montreal. Acquired by GSK in 2023 for about 2 billion USD. Customers would have been patients with chronic cough treated by respiratory specialists. Research-stage company with no consumer awareness.

US-Israeli specialty pharma that developed Mycapssa, an oral octreotide capsule for acromegaly, a rare hormone disorder caused by a pituitary tumour, using a transient permeability enhancer technology. Listed on Nasdaq (CHMA), it was acquired by Irish rare disease firm Amryt Pharma in 2021. Customers are endocrinologists and patients who previously needed injections. Small drug company with no consumer awareness beyond patient communities.

about: Chinese biotechnology company developing vaccines and biologics, best known for SCB-2019, a recombinant COVID-19 spike protein vaccine candidate with a protein adjuvant, tested in large international trials. Also works on RSV and shingles vaccines. Listed in Hong Kong in 2021 and operates from Chengdu, Shanghai and Australia. Customers are governments and health systems. Research-focused firm with limited consumer awareness, though known to specialists during the pandemic.

about: US renewable chemicals company, founded in 2008 in San Diego, that uses fermentation to make bio-based chemicals such as butanediol (BDO) from sugar and plant feedstock instead of fossil fuels, and the Brevano bio-nylon. Customers are chemical makers and consumer brands, including apparel partners such as Lululemon, who pay for licensed processes and product. Raised significant venture funding. B2B materials brand with growing profile in sustainable fashion.
